I-Physical principles
1-Concept of partial pressure
Atmospheric air is a mixture of gases.
Normally air contains 79% nitrogen (N2), 21% O2, a negligible percentage of CO2, rare gases, atmospheric pollutants and water vapor.
All together, these gases exert a total atmospheric pressure (Patm) of 760mmHg on average at sea level.

I-Physical principles
1-Concept of partial pressure
The partial pressure is the pressure exerted individually by each gas (Pgaz).

According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the pressures exerted by each of the constituent gases and can be expressed by the following equation:
Partial pressure of a gas = total pressure (PA)

2-Diffusion of gases in liquids
According to Henry's Law, when a liquid is exposed to a gas mixture, each gas dissolves in the liquid in proportion to its partial pressure.
Therefore, the more concentrated a gas is in the gas mixture, the more and more quickly it dissolves in the liquid.
At the equilibrium point, the partial pressures of the gases are the same in both phases.

IV-Gas exchanges in systemic capillaries
The transfer of O2 and CO2 between blood in systemic capillaries and tissue cells occurs by simple diffusion due to differences in partial pressures.
The arterial blood arriving in the systemic capillaries is practically identical to that leaving the lungs through the pulmonary veins: the PO2 is 100mm Hg and the PCO2 is 40mm Hg.

Differences in PO2 and PCO2 at the level of systemic capillaries:
Due to oxidative metabolism, cells consume O2 and produce CO2 continuously:
-the cellular PO2 is around 40mm Hg (it is much lower in the mitochondria, the seat of oxidative metabolism);
-the PCO2 is 46 mm Hg (these values ​​vary depending on the level of activity of oxidative metabolism).
The O2 then diffuses under the effect of the difference in PO2 (from the systemic capillaries to the cells).
IV-Gas exchanges in systemic capillaries
The opposite happens for CO2.
This diffuses rapidly out of the cells (PCO2 = 46 mmHg) towards the blood entering the capillaries (PCO2 = 40mmHg): difference in partial pressure linked to the continuous production of CO2.
This transfer of CO2 continues until the PCO2 of the blood is in balance with that of the tissues, i.e. 46mm Hg.
Systemic venous blood, which is relatively low in O2 (PO2 = 40mm Hg) and rich in CO2 (PCO2 = 46 mm Hg), returns to the heart which pumps it to the lungs.

GENERAL Definition
The main function of respiration is to ensure gas exchanges: intake of O₂ and elimination of CO₂ = respiratory activity is rhythmic, automatic and permanent.
Ventilatory activity is generated by neural networks in the brainstem
The objective of ventilatory regulation is to maintain homeostasis by ensuring the stability of partial pressures in O2 (PaO₂), CO2 (PaCO₂) as well as blood pH, within narrow limits.
It thus makes it possible to constantly adapt the frequency and amplitude of respiratory movements to the needs of the body.
GENERAL Respiratory control
Respiratory automation:
- Modular according to the needs of the organization
- Coordination with other functions: Swallowing, Phonation
factors modulating respiration:
- metabolic activity: sleep, physical exercise

Afferent pathways: transmit information from receptors to respiratory centers
Respiratory centers: integrate and coordinate information
Efferent pathways: from respiratory centers to muscles

In normal subjects, each contraction is triggered in the sinus node (normal sinus rhythm). The frequency decreases (bradycardia) during sleep and increases (tachycardia) under the influence of emotions, exercise, fever and many other stimuli.
Dysfunction of the NSA, induced by drugs or diseases, can reduce or even eliminate the transmission of PA from the atria to the ventricles.

In this case, the cells capable of autorhythmicity of the AVN, the His bundle and the Purkinje network, which are no longer driven by the NSA, begin to generate excitations at their own inherent rhythm, thus becoming the pacemaker of the ventricles. This rhythm is quite slow, from 25 to 40 beats/min.

The current treatment for all severe atrioventricular conduction disorders, as well as many other abnormal rhythms, is the permanent surgical implantation of an artificial pacemaker that electrically stimulates the ventricular cells at a normal rhythm.

Conclusion

In the heart, contractions are controlled by a well-regulated cascade of electrical signal transmission that begins in the NSA and passes through the atrial muscle tissue and then throughout the conduction tissue to reach the ventricles. The propagation of the electrical signal from one cell to another takes place through gap junctions. The speed of propagation depends on anatomical characteristics, but it can also be modified by a nerve impulse.

INTRODUCTION
The thymus is a large odd and medial primary (central) epithelial organ located in the upper part of the anterior mediastinum.
-10 to 15 g at birth, 30 to 40 g at puberty then progressive involution
-Consisted of two lobes divided into incomplete lobules
-Organ where immature (prothymocytes) and naive T lymphocytes from the bone marrow differentiate into mature lymphocytes.

Histophysiology
-the thymus ensures lymphopoiesis of T cells.
-the epithelial reticular cells of the thymic framework provide 3 essential functions:
-support for the thymic parenchyma.

-secretion of several hormonal factors acting on lymphopoiesis including lymphopoietin which induces the differentiation of parent cells into T lymphocytes or thymocytes and the maturation of the latter into immunologically competent cells.
-direct role in immunity (rejection of transplants).
○ auxiliaries or CD4 which promote the humoral response by stimulating the B
○ cytotoxic (CD8): kill tumor or infected cells
○ suppressors (CD8): inhibit the humoral response
○ NK (Natural Killer) cells
○ Secrete cytokines
○ Express an antigen receptor
conclusion
The thymus is made up of cells: lymphoid, epithelial, macrophage and dendritic cells allowing the maturation of thymocytes.
The function of the thymus is to ensure the development and maturation of T lymphocytes.
